15. Optimization & Machine Learning: Advanced Topics

CNRS & DMA, École Normale Supérieure

Chapter PDF · Complete book

Reliable and efficient learning requires control of model complexity, economical use of large datasets, and accurate derivative calculations. We study regularization through ridge regression and sparsity, followed by stochastic gradient methods that reduce the cost of individual updates. The final section derives automatic differentiation on computational graphs and applies it to feedforward networks, recurrent models, and optimization procedures.

15.1 Regularization¶

When the sample size nnn is small relative to the model dimension ppp, regularization helps control the complexity of empirical risk minimization.

15.1.1 Penalized Least Squares¶

For simplicity, consider regularized least-squares regression:

min⁡x∈Rp  fλ(x):=12∣ ⁣∣Ax−y∣ ⁣∣2+λR(x)(15.1)\underset{x \in \mathbb{R}^p}{\min}\; f_\lambda(x) \mathrel{:=}\frac{1}{2}|\!| Ax-y |\!|^2 + \lambda R(x) \tag{15.1}x∈Rpmin​fλ​(x):=21​∣∣Ax−y∣∣2+λR(x)(15.1)

where R(x)R(x)R(x) is the regularizer and λ⩾0\lambda\geqslant 0λ⩾0 the regularization parameter.

The regularizer expresses prior structure of the weight vector xxx, such as small magnitude or sparsity. The strength λ\lambdaλ can be selected by cross-validation.

We assume that RRR is finite, nonnegative, lower semicontinuous, and coercive, i.e. R(x)→+∞R(x) \rightarrow +\inftyR(x)→+∞ as ∣ ⁣∣x∣ ⁣∣→+∞|\!| x |\!| \rightarrow +\infty∣∣x∣∣→+∞.

The following proposition shows that as λ↓0\lambda\downarrow0λ↓0, regularization selects among the exact solutions when Ax=yAx=yAx=y is feasible. This is particularly useful when ker⁡(A)≠{0}\ker(A)\neq\{0\}ker(A)={0} and there are infinitely many exact solutions.

Proposition 15.1

Assume Ax=yAx=yAx=y is feasible and λk>0\lambda_k>0λk​>0 tends to zero. If xλkx_{\lambda_k}xλk​​ minimizes fλkf_{\lambda_k}fλk​​, then this sequence is bounded, and every accumulation point x⋆x^\starx⋆ is a solution of the constrained optimization problem

Proof

Choose an arbitrary feasible point x0x_0x0​, so Ax0=yAx_0=yAx0​=y. Optimality of xλkx_{\lambda_k}xλk​​ gives

12∣ ⁣∣Axλk−y∣ ⁣∣2+λkR(xλk)⩽λkR(x0).(15.3)\frac{1}{2}|\!| Ax_{\lambda_k}-y |\!|^2 + \lambda_k R(x_{\lambda_k}) \leqslant\lambda_k R(x_0). \tag{15.3}21​∣∣Axλk​​−y∣∣2+λk​R(xλk​​)⩽λk​R(x0​).(15.3)

15.1.3 Lasso¶

The Lasso uses an ℓ1\ell^1ℓ1 penalty:

R(x)=∣ ⁣∣x∣ ⁣∣1:=∑k=1p∣xk∣.R(x) = |\!| x |\!|_1 \mathrel{:=}\sum_{k=1}^p |x_k|.R(x)=∣∣x∣∣1​:=k=1∑p​∣xk​∣.

The penalty promotes sparsity in the solutions xλx_\lambdaxλ​ of

xλ∈argminx∈Rp  fλ(x)=12∣ ⁣∣Ax−y∣ ⁣∣Rn2+λ∣ ⁣∣x∣ ⁣∣1x_\lambda\in \underset{x \in \mathbb{R}^p}{\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}}\; f_\lambda(x) = \frac{1}{2} |\!| Ax-y |\!|^2_{\mathbb{R}^n} + \lambda|\!| x |\!|_1xλ​∈x∈Rpargmin​fλ​(x)=21​∣∣Ax−y∣∣Rn2​+λ∣∣x∣∣1​

The solutions xλx_\lambdaxλ​ may be nonunique, and typically have many zero coefficients.

Figure 15.1 illustrates the geometry of ℓq\ell^qℓq balls. They concentrate around the coordinate axes as q→0q \rightarrow 0q→0, favoring sparse solutions, but become nonconvex for q<1q<1q<1.

Sparsity can encode a prior on the unknown, as in imaging, or select a small subset of predictive features. Feature selection can make a model easier to interpret and cheaper to evaluate.

Whether Lasso or ridge regression performs better depends on sparsity, correlations, noise, and the prediction task.

The objective fλf_\lambdafλ​ is convex, but the ℓ1\ell^1ℓ1 penalty is nonsmooth, so ordinary gradient descent does not apply at all points.

Section 15.1.4 develops an appropriate modification of gradient descent.

A closed-form solution xλx_\lambdaxλ​ is generally unavailable, but the case of an orthogonal design matrix AAA reduces to coordinatewise thresholding.

The term K(x,x′)K(x,x')K(x,x′) is nonnegative when λmax⁡(A⊤A)⩽1/τ\lambda_{\max}(A^\top A) \leqslant 1/\tauλmax​(A⊤A)⩽1/τ, equivalently τ⩽1/∣ ⁣∣A∣ ⁣∣op2\tau \leqslant 1/|\!| A |\!|_{\text{op}}^2τ⩽1/∣∣A∣∣op2​, where ∣ ⁣∣A∣ ⁣∣op=σmax⁡(A)|\!| A |\!|_{\text{op}} = \sigma_{\max}(A)∣∣A∣∣op​=σmax​(A) is the operator norm.

f(x)⩽fτ(x,x′),fτ(x,x)=f(x),andf(⋅)−fτ(⋅,x′) is smooth.f(x) \leqslant f_\tau(x,x'), \quad f_\tau(x,x)=f(x), \quad \text{and} \quad f(\cdot)-f_\tau(\cdot,x') \text{ is smooth.}f(x)⩽fτ​(x,x′),fτ​(x,x)=f(x),andf(⋅)−fτ​(⋅,x′) is smooth.

15.2 Stochastic Optimization¶

We study stochastic gradient methods for large datasets of size nnn and for objectives defined as expectations.

15.2.1 Minimizing Sums and Expectations¶

Many learning objectives are finite averages:

min⁡x∈Rp  f(x):=1n∑i=1nfi(x)(15.8)\underset{x \in \mathbb{R}^p}{\min}\; f(x) \mathrel{:=}\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x) \tag{15.8}x∈Rpmin​f(x):=n1​i=1∑n​fi​(x)(15.8)

or expectations:

min⁡x∈Rp  f(x):=Ez∼π(f(x,z))=∫Zf(x,z)dπ(z).(15.9)\underset{x \in \mathbb{R}^p}{\min}\; f(x) \mathrel{:=}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim \pi}( f(x,\mathbf{z}) ) = \int_{\mathcal{Z}} f(x,z) \mathrm{d}\pi(z). \tag{15.9}x∈Rpmin​f(x):=Ez∼π​(f(x,z))=∫Z​f(x,z)dπ(z).(15.9)

A finite average is an expectation under the uniform measure π=1n∑i=1nδi\pi=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_iπ=n1​∑i=1n​δi​, with f(x,i)=fi(x)f(x,i)=f_i(x)f(x,i)=fi​(x). Conversely, drawing (zi)i(z_i)_i(zi​)i​ i.i.d. from π\piπ and setting fi(x)=f(x,zi)f_i(x)=f(x,z_i)fi​(x)=f(x,zi​) gives an empirical approximation of (15.9). Under integrability, the empirical objective converges pointwise by the law of large numbers. Convergence of minima or minimizers requires additional assumptions.

For example, empirical risk minimization with linear predictors uses

fi(x)=ℓ(⟨ai, x⟩,yi)andf(x,z)=ℓ(⟨a, x⟩,y)(15.10)f_i(x) = \ell(\langle a_i,\,x\rangle,y_i) \quad \text{and} \quad f(x,z) = \ell(\langle a,\,x\rangle,y) \tag{15.10}fi​(x)=ℓ(⟨ai​,x⟩,yi​)andf(x,z)=ℓ(⟨a,x⟩,y)(15.10)

for z=(a,y)∈Z=(A=Rp)×Yz=(a,y) \in \mathcal{Z}= (\mathcal{A}=\mathbb{R}^p) \times \mathcal{Y}z=(a,y)∈Z=(A=Rp)×Y (typically Y=R\mathcal{Y}=\mathbb{R}Y=R or Y={−1,+1}\mathcal{Y}=\{-1,+1\}Y={−1,+1} for regression and classification), where ℓ\ellℓ is some loss function.

We illustrate the methods with binary logistic classification, using

L(s,y):=log⁡(1+exp⁡(−sy)).(15.11)L(s,y) \mathrel{:=}\log( 1+\exp(-sy) ). \tag{15.11}L(s,y):=log(1+exp(−sy)).(15.11)

The same computational approach extends to general parametric models, including deep neural networks.

The stochastic methods below apply both to finite sums (15.8) and to expectations (15.9), under the corresponding unbiasedness and moment assumptions. We present them for finite sums. When nnn is large, the aim is to make each iteration inexpensive without evaluating every summand.

When the summands fi(x)f_i(x)fi​(x) are similar, a single gradient can approximate the average well: ∇fi≈∇f\nabla f_i \approx \nabla f∇fi​≈∇f. Evaluating ∇fi\nabla f_i∇fi​ is typically nnn times cheaper than forming the full gradient.

Stochastic optimization is nevertheless not always faster than batch gradient descent.

For moderate nnn, a deterministic method may use the available computation more effectively.

When nnn is too large for a full pass to be practical, stochastic methods divide the work into small updates and begin improving the model immediately. Mini-batches also permit parallel computation.

15.2.2 Batch Gradient Descent (BGD)¶

Batch gradient descent (BGD), analyzed in Section 14.4, iterates

xk+1=xk−τk∇f(xk)x_{k+1} = x_k - \tau_k \nabla f(x_k)xk+1​=xk​−τk​∇f(xk​)

For a convex objective with an LLL-Lipschitz gradient and a minimizer, the condition 0<τmin⁡⩽τk⩽τmax⁡<2/L0<\tau_{\min}\leqslant\tau_k\leqslant\tau_{\max}<2/L0<τmin​⩽τk​⩽τmax​<2/L ensures convergence. Strong convexity strengthens this to a linear rate.

For a finite-sum objective, the gradient is

∇f(x)=1n∑i=1n∇fi(x)(15.12)\nabla f(x) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \nabla f_i(x) \tag{15.12}∇f(x)=n1​i=1∑n​∇fi​(x)(15.12)

Its cost is typically O(np)O(np)O(np) when each ∇fi\nabla f_i∇fi​ can be evaluated in time linear in ppp.

For an ERM summand of the form (15.10), Taylor expansion gives

∇fi(x)=ℓ′(⟨ai, x⟩,yi)ai.(15.13)\nabla f_i(x) = \ell'( \langle a_i,\,x\rangle,y_i ) a_i. \tag{15.13}∇fi​(x)=ℓ′(⟨ai​,x⟩,yi​)ai​.(15.13)

15.2.3 Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD)¶

Figure 15.4. Unbiased stochastic gradient estimate (panel 1) and a schematic SGD trajectory (panel 2).

For very large nnn, computing the full gradient ∇f\nabla f∇f as in (15.12) is prohibitive.

SGD replaces the full gradient by the gradient of one summand fif_{i}fi​, with iii sampled uniformly. This gives an unbiased estimate:

Ei∇fi(x)=∇f(x)(15.14)\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{i}}{ \nabla f_{\mathbf{i}}(x) } = \nabla f(x) \tag{15.14}Ei​∇fi​(x)=∇f(x)(15.14)

where i\mathbf{i}i is a random variable distributed uniformly in {1,…,n}\{1,\ldots,n\}{1,…,n}.

Starting from x0x_0x0​, stochastic gradient descent (SGD) iterates

xk+1=xk−τk∇fi(k)(xk)x_{k+1} = x_k - \tau_k \nabla f_{i(k)}(x_k)xk+1​=xk​−τk​∇fi(k)​(xk​)

where, for each iteration index kkk, i(k)i(k)i(k) is drawn independently of previous draws, uniformly from {1,…,n}\{1,\ldots,n\}{1,…,n}.

The iterates xk+1x_{k+1}xk+1​ are random. We therefore study convergence to a minimizer of fff in a probabilistic sense, such as mean square or probability, together with the corresponding rates.

A batch-gradient step costs O(np)O(np)O(np), whereas an SGD step costs O(p)O(p)O(p). This makes SGD attractive when nnn is large and repeated passes through the data are costly. Redundancy between observations can sometimes yield accurate predictions after only k≪nk \ll nk≪n updates, before all observations have been used.

The step-size schedule τk\tau_kτk​ must balance two requirements: it usually needs to decrease to suppress stochastic noise, but not so quickly that the method stops making progress before reaching a minimizer.

A common schedule has asymptotic behavior τk∼k−1\tau_k \sim k^{-1}τk​∼k−1 as k→+∞k\rightarrow +\inftyk→+∞. One such schedule is

τk:=τ01+k/k0(15.15)\tau_k \mathrel{:=}\frac{\tau_0}{1 + k/k_0} \tag{15.15}τk​:=1+k/k0​τ0​​(15.15)

where τ0>0\tau_0>0τ0​>0 sets the initial step and k0>0k_0>0k0​>0 controls how long the steps remain approximately constant.

Figure 15.5 illustrates minimization of f1(x)+f2(x)f_1(x)+f_2(x)f1​(x)+f2​(x) for x∈Rx \in \mathbb{R}x∈R, with f1(x)=(x−1)2f_1(x)=(x-1)^2f1​(x)=(x−1)2 and f2(x)=(x+1)2f_2(x)=(x+1)^2f2​(x)=(x+1)2. The distribution of xkx_kxk​ concentrates around the minimizer x⋆=0x^\star=0x⋆=0. The initial iterate x0x_0x0​ is uniform on [−1/2,1/2][-1/2,1/2][−1/2,1/2].

The preceding SGD bound, and the averaging scheme below, give sublinear rates even when fff is strongly convex. By contrast, batch gradient descent has a linear rate under the assumptions of Theorem 14.16.

15.2.4 Stochastic Gradient Descent with Averaging (SGA)¶

Diminishing steps can slow SGD as τk\tau_kτk​ approaches zero.

Averaging reduces fluctuations in the estimate. Run SGD on auxiliary iterates (x~k)k( \tilde x_k)_k(x~k​)k​,

x~k+1=x~k−τk∇fi(k)(x~k)\tilde x_{k+1}=\tilde x_k - \tau_k \nabla f_{i(k)}(\tilde x_k)x~k+1​=x~k​−τk​∇fi(k)​(x~k​)

and return their Cesàro average:

xk:=1k∑ℓ=1kx~ℓ.x_k \mathrel{:=}\frac{1}{k} \sum_{\ell=1}^k \tilde x_{\ell}.xk​:=k1​ℓ=1∑k​x~ℓ​.

This gives stochastic gradient descent with averaging (SGA), also called averaged SGD.

The average can be maintained without storing the full trajectory, using the recursive update

xk+1=1k+1x~k+1+kk+1xk.x_{k+1}=\frac{1}{k+1}\tilde x_{k+1}+\frac{k}{k+1}x_k.xk+1​=k+11​x~k+1​+k+1k​xk​.

A typical step-size schedule is

τk:=τ01+k/k0.\tau_k \mathrel{:=}\frac{\tau_0}{1 + \sqrt{k/k_0}}.τk​:=1+k/k0​​τ0​​.

These steps decrease more slowly, at rate k−1/2k^{-1/2}k−1/2.

Averaging can reduce sensitivity to the tuning parameters (k0,τ0)(k_0,\tau_0)(k0​,τ0​), although their choice still affects performance.

Bach proves that for logistic classification, averaging can adapt to local curvature under suitable regularity and step-size assumptions. This is a problem-dependent result, rather than a universal improvement of every constant over SGD.

15.2.5 Stochastic Averaged Gradient Descent (SAG)¶

For a finite dataset with nnn samples of total size n×pn \times pn×p, one can trade additional memory for reduced gradient noise by storing past gradient evaluations. This yields the stochastic averaged gradient (SAG) method.

Store the latest gradient of each summand in a table (Gi)i=1n(G^i)_{i=1}^n(Gi)i=1n​, requiring O(np)O(np)O(np) memory. Maintain its average ggg as an approximation to the full gradient.

Initialize Gi=0G^i=0Gi=0 for all iii and g=0g=0g=0, so that g=n−1∑iGig=n^{-1}\sum_iG^ig=n−1∑i​Gi is the stored average. At each iteration, update the table and then xxx:

xk+1=xk−τgwhere{h←∇fi(k)(xk),g←g+1n(h−Gi(k)),Gi(k)←h.x_{k+1} = x_k - \tau g \quad \text{where} \quad \left\{ \begin{array}{l} h\leftarrow\nabla f_{i(k)}(x_k), \\ g\leftarrow g+\frac 1n(h-G^{i(k)}), \\ G^{i(k)} \leftarrow h. \end{array} \right.xk+1​=xk​−τgwhere⎩⎨⎧​h←∇fi(k)​(xk​),g←g+n1​(h−Gi(k)),Gi(k)←h.​

Because most entries were evaluated at earlier iterates, the table average is generally biased conditional on the current history. Its convergence analysis therefore differs from the unbiased-SGD proof above. SAG uses a fixed step size τ\tauτ. As for batch gradient descent, choose τ\tauτ on the scale of 1/L1/L1/L, where LLL bounds the Lipschitz constants of the individual gradients ∇fi\nabla f_i∇fi​; the admissible numerical constant depends on the convergence theorem.

For smooth convex finite sums with a minimizer and a suitable step size, SAG admits an O(1/k)O(1/k)O(1/k) expected objective bound for averaged iterates. Furthermore, in the presence of strong convexity (for instance after adding a positive quadratic penalty to logistic regression), it has a linear convergence rate, i.e.

E(f(xk))−f(x⋆)=O(ρk),\mathbb{E}( f(x_k) ) - f(x^\star) = O\left( \rho^k \right),E(f(xk​))−f(x⋆)=O(ρk),

for some 0<ρ<10 < \rho < 10<ρ<1.

These improvements exploit the finite-sum structure: SAG stores information about each of the nnn summands. SGD and averaged SGD also extend beyond finite nnn to general expectations (15.9).

15.3 Automatic Differentiation¶

Gradient evaluation ∇f(x)\nabla f(x)∇f(x) is the main operation in batch and stochastic gradient methods. For linear models and shallow networks, explicit formulas usually reduce it to matrix-vector products. For deeper or more elaborate computations, expanded derivative formulas become unwieldy and can duplicate work. Automatic differentiation organizes the chain rule recursively to reuse intermediate results.

15.3.1 Finite Differences and Symbolic Calculus¶

For f:Rp→Rf : \mathbb{R}^p \rightarrow \mathbb{R}f:Rp→R, we want to evaluate ∇f:Rp↦Rp\nabla f : \mathbb{R}^p \mapsto \mathbb{R}^p∇f:Rp↦Rp. A finite-difference approximation with a small parameter ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0 is

1ε(f(x+εδ1)−f(x),…,f(x+εδp)−f(x))⊤≈∇f(x)\frac{1}{\varepsilon}(f(x+\varepsilon\delta_1)-f(x), \ldots,f(x+\varepsilon\delta_p)-f(x))^\top \approx \nabla f(x)ε1​(f(x+εδ1​)−f(x),…,f(x+εδp​)−f(x))⊤≈∇f(x)

This requires p+1p+1p+1 evaluations of fff. Here δk=(0,…,0,1,0,…,0)\delta_k=(0,\ldots,0,1,0,\ldots,0)δk​=(0,…,0,1,0,…,0) is the coordinate vector with its 1 at position kkk.

For large ppp, repeated evaluations are expensive. Finite differences also balance truncation error against floating-point cancellation as ε\varepsilonε decreases. Reverse-mode automatic differentiation computes the full gradient at a cost typically proportional to one evaluation of fff.

Like symbolic differentiation, automatic differentiation applies exact derivative rules, subject to floating-point error. It organizes those rules around the operations of the program that evaluates the function, preserving reuse of intermediate computations.

15.3.2 Computational Graphs¶

Let x=(x1,…,xs)x=(x_1,\ldots,x_s)x=(x1​,…,xs​) be the inputs to a program evaluating fff. Number its intermediate variables xs+1,…,xtx_{s+1},\ldots,x_txs+1​,…,xt​, with output xt=f(x)x_t=f(x)xt​=f(x), and let xk∈Rnkx_k\in\mathbb{R}^{n_k}xk​∈Rnk​. We seek the Jacobian blocks ∂f(x)∂xk∈Rnt×nk\frac{ \partial f(x)}{\partial x_k} \in\mathbb{R}^{n_t\times n_k}∂xk​∂f(x)​∈Rnt​×nk​ for k=1,…,sk=1,\ldots,sk=1,…,s. The scalar case nk=1n_k=1nk​=1 is easiest to follow; the formulas also apply to vector variables if the matrix products retain the displayed order. The total input dimension is p=∑k=1snkp=\sum_{k=1}^s n_kp=∑k=1s​nk​.

Figure 15.8. A computational graph.

Represent the computation as a sequence of elementary maps:

∀ k=s+1,…,t,xk=fk(x1,…,xk−1)\forall \,k=s+1,\ldots,t, \quad x_k = f_k( x_1,\ldots,x_{k-1} )∀k=s+1,…,t,xk​=fk​(x1​,…,xk−1​)

Each fkf_kfk​ depends only on earlier variables; see Figure 15.8. The directed acyclic graph (DAG) connects each argument used by fkf_kfk​ to its output xkx_kxk​. The indexing is a topological order: every edge points from a smaller to a larger index.

Evaluating f(x)f(x)f(x) is a forward traversal of the graph.

Automatic differentiation differentiates the supplied computational graph. It does not by itself choose an efficient implementation of the original formula; the derivative computation benefits from the efficiency and reuse already present in the forward program.

15.3.3 Forward Mode of Automatic Differentiation¶

Forward mode propagates derivatives of each intermediate variable with respect to a chosen input block, here x1x_1x1​. For scalar inputs, repeating the traversal for all ppp coordinates gives the full derivative. The formulas below also propagate a block Jacobian when n1>1n_1>1n1​>1.

Figure 15.9. Derivative dependencies in forward mode (left) and reverse mode (right).

Initialize the input derivatives by

∂x1∂x1=Idn1×n1,∂x2∂x1=0n2×n1,…,∂xs∂x1=0ns×n1,\frac{ \partial x_1}{\partial x_1} = \mathrm{Id}_{n_1 \times n_1}, \quad \frac{ \partial x_2}{\partial x_1} = 0_{n_2 \times n_1}, \ldots, \quad \frac{ \partial x_s}{\partial x_1} = 0_{n_s \times n_1},∂x1​∂x1​​=Idn1​×n1​​,∂x1​∂x2​​=0n2​×n1​​,…,∂x1​∂xs​​=0ns​×n1​​,

These are one and zero for scalar inputs. Propagate the derivatives using

∀ k=s+1,…,t,∂xk∂x1=∑ℓ∈parent(k)[∂xk∂xℓ]×∂xℓ∂x1=∑ℓ∈parent(k)∂fk∂xℓ(x1,…,xk−1)×∂xℓ∂x1.\forall \,k=s+1,\ldots,t, \quad \frac{ \partial x_k}{\partial x_1} = \sum_{\ell \in \text{parent}(k)} \left[ \frac{ \partial x_k}{\partial x_\ell} \right] \times \frac{ \partial x_\ell}{\partial x_1} = \sum_{\ell \in \text{parent}(k)} \frac{ \partial f_k}{\partial x_\ell} (x_1,\ldots,x_{k-1}) \times \frac{ \partial x_\ell}{\partial x_1} .∀k=s+1,…,t,∂x1​∂xk​​=ℓ∈parent(k)∑​[∂xℓ​∂xk​​]×∂x1​∂xℓ​​=ℓ∈parent(k)∑​∂xℓ​∂fk​​(x1​,…,xk−1​)×∂x1​∂xℓ​​.

The notation “parent(k)\text{parent}(k)parent(k)” denotes the nodes ℓ<k\ell<kℓ<k of the graph that are connected to kkk, see Figure 15.9, left.

The stored quantities are the derivatives ∂xℓ∂x1\frac{ \partial x_\ell}{\partial x_1}∂x1​∂xℓ​​. The symbol ×\times× denotes matrix multiplication in the vector-valued case.

The brackets […][\ldots][…] indicate a local derivative: ∂xk∂xℓ\frac{ \partial x_k}{\partial x_\ell}∂xℓ​∂xk​​ is the derivative of the elementary map fkf_kfk​ with respect to that argument. It can be evaluated when needed, assuming the local derivative is available in closed form.

Suppose the local derivative operations ∂fk∂xℓ\frac{ \partial f_k}{\partial x_\ell}∂xℓ​∂fk​​ have comparable costs, as when the variable dimensions nkn_knk​ are uniformly bounded, and each node has a bounded number of parents. Computing the full Jacobian coordinate by coordinate requires ppp traversals, each with cost comparable to a forward evaluation. This becomes expensive for large ppp.

Simple example.

We consider the function

f(x,y)=ylog⁡(x)+ylog⁡(x)(15.19)f(x,y) = y\log(x)+\sqrt{y\log(x)} \tag{15.19}f(x,y)=ylog(x)+ylog(x)​(15.19)

on the open domain x>0x>0x>0, ylog⁡x>0y\log x>0ylogx>0, where all elementary derivatives exist. Its computational graph is displayed in Figure 15.10. The iterations of the forward mode to compute the derivative with respect to xxx read

Dual numbers.

Dual numbers provide a convenient implementation of the forward pass. They form a real algebra whose elements have the form x+εx′x + \varepsilon x'x+εx′ where ε\varepsilonε is a symbol obeying the rule that ε2=0\varepsilon^2=0ε2=0. Here (x,x′)∈R2(x,x') \in \mathbb{R}^2(x,x′)∈R2 and x′x'x′ is intended to store a derivative with respect to some input variable. Multiplication and, when x≠0x\neq0x=0, inversion are given by

(x+εx′)(y+εy′)=xy+ε(xy′+yx′)and1x+εx′=1x−εx′x2.(x+\varepsilon x')(y+\varepsilon y') = xy + \varepsilon(x y' + y x') \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{1}{x+\varepsilon x'} = \frac{1}{x}-\varepsilon\frac{x'}{x^2}.(x+εx′)(y+εy′)=xy+ε(xy′+yx′)andx+εx′1​=x1​−εx2x′​.

For polynomial or rational fff, the arithmetic rules imply

f(x+ε)=f(x)+εf′(x).f(x+\varepsilon) = f(x) + \varepsilon f'(x).f(x+ε)=f(x)+εf′(x).

For another differentiable elementary function fff, define its action on dual numbers by

f(x+εx′):=f(x)+εf′(x)x′.f(x+\varepsilon x') \mathrel{:=}f(x) + \varepsilon f'(x) x'.f(x+εx′):=f(x)+εf′(x)x′.

This definition gives

(f∘g)(x+ε)=f(g(x))+εf′(g(x))g′(x)(f \circ g)(x+\varepsilon) = f(g(x)) + \varepsilon f'(g(x))g'(x)(f∘g)(x+ε)=f(g(x))+εf′(g(x))g′(x)

which is the chain rule. More generally, for f(x1,…,xs)f(x_1,\ldots,x_s)f(x1​,…,xs​) built from these elementary operations,

f(x1+ε,x2,…,xs)=f(x1,…,xs)+ε∂f∂x1(x1,…,xs)f(x_1+\varepsilon,x_2,\ldots,x_s) = f(x_1,\ldots,x_s) + \varepsilon \frac{ \partial f}{\partial x_1} (x_1,\ldots,x_s)f(x1​+ε,x2​,…,xs​)=f(x1​,…,xs​)+ε∂x1​∂f​(x1​,…,xs​)

the dual-number evaluation computes ∂f∂x1(x1,…,xs)\frac{ \partial f}{\partial x_1} (x_1,\ldots,x_s)∂x1​∂f​(x1​,…,xs​) by forward-mode differentiation. The other coordinates are treated identically.

15.3.4 Reverse Mode of Automatic Differentiation¶

Reverse mode computes the derivatives ∂xt∂xk\frac{ \partial x_t}{\partial x_k}∂xk​∂xt​​ of the output with respect to the intermediate variables. For a scalar output and many input coordinates, this avoids the repeated forward traversals required to compute each ∂xk∂xi\frac{ \partial x_k}{\partial x_i}∂xi​∂xk​​ separately.

Initialize the derivative of the output node by

∂xt∂xt=Idnt×nt,\frac{ \partial x_t}{\partial x_t} = \mathrm{Id}_{n_t \times n_t},∂xt​∂xt​​=Idnt​×nt​​,

and apply the following recursion from the last node to the first:

∀ k=t−1,t−2,…,1,∂xt∂xk=∑m∈son(k)∂xt∂xm×[∂xm∂xk]=∑m∈son(k)∂xt∂xm×∂fm(x1,…,xm−1)∂xk.\forall \,k=t-1,t-2,\ldots,1, \quad \frac{ \partial x_t}{\partial x_k} = \sum_{m \in \text{son}(k)} \frac{ \partial x_t}{\partial x_m} \times \left[ \frac{ \partial x_m}{\partial x_k} \right] = \sum_{m \in \text{son}(k)} \frac{ \partial x_t}{\partial x_m} \times \frac{ \partial f_m(x_1,\ldots,x_{m-1})}{\partial x_k} .∀k=t−1,t−2,…,1,∂xk​∂xt​​=m∈son(k)∑​∂xm​∂xt​​×[∂xk​∂xm​​]=m∈son(k)∑​∂xm​∂xt​​×∂xk​∂fm​(x1​,…,xm−1​)​.

The set son(k)\text{son}(k)son(k) contains the children m>km>km>k that depend directly on xkx_kxk​, as shown in Figure 15.9, right. Contributions from every child must be added.

Back-propagation.

For a scalar output xt∈Rx_t \in \mathbb{R}xt​∈R, we have ∂xt∂xk=[∇xkf(x)]⊤∈R1×nk\frac{ \partial x_t}{\partial x_k} = [\nabla_{x_k} f(x)]^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times n_k}∂xk​∂xt​​=[∇xk​​f(x)]⊤∈R1×nk​. The reverse recursion can then be written for gradient vectors:

∀ k=t−1,t−2,…,1,∇xkf(x)=∑m∈son(k)(∂fm(x1,…,xm−1)∂xk)⊤(∇xmf(x)).\forall \,k=t-1,t-2,\ldots,1, \quad \nabla_{x_k} f(x) = \sum_{m \in \text{son}(k)} \left( \frac{ \partial f_m(x_1,\ldots,x_{m-1})}{\partial x_k} \right)^\top \left( \nabla_{x_m} f(x) \right).∀k=t−1,t−2,…,1,∇xk​​f(x)=m∈son(k)∑​(∂xk​∂fm​(x1​,…,xm−1​)​)⊤(∇xm​​f(x)).

Here (∂fm(x1,…,xm−1)∂xk)⊤∈Rnk×nm\left( \frac{ \partial f_m(x_1,\ldots,x_{m-1})}{\partial x_k} \right)^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{n_k \times n_m}(∂xk​∂fm​(x1​,…,xm−1​)​)⊤∈Rnk​×nm​ is the adjoint Jacobian of fmf_mfm​. This adjoint recursion is called backpropagation and is the standard form used in machine learning.

For a scalar output (nt=1n_t=1nt​=1), reverse mode is usually the preferred way to compute the full gradient. It requires access to the intermediate variables (xk)k=s+1t(x_k)_{k=s+1}^t(xk​)k=s+1t​, which can be costly to store for a large graph. Checkpointing trades additional computation for reduced storage.

∂f∂f=1∂f∂c=∂f∂f[∂f∂c]=∂f∂f1{c↦f=b+c}∂f∂b=∂f∂c[∂c∂b]+∂f∂f[∂f∂b]=∂f∂c12b+∂f∂f1{b↦c=b,b↦f=b+c}∂f∂a=∂f∂b[∂b∂a]=∂f∂by{a↦b=ya}∂f∂y=∂f∂b[∂b∂y]=∂f∂ba{y↦b=ya}∂f∂x=∂f∂a[∂a∂x]=∂f∂a1x{x↦a=log⁡(x)}\begin{aligned} \frac{ \partial f}{\partial f} &= 1 &\\ \frac{ \partial f}{\partial c} &= \frac{ \partial f}{\partial f} \left[ \frac{ \partial f}{\partial c} \right] = \frac{ \partial f}{\partial f} 1 & \{ c \mapsto f = b+c\}\\ \frac{ \partial f}{\partial b} &= \frac{ \partial f}{\partial c} \left[ \frac{ \partial c}{\partial b} \right] + \frac{ \partial f}{\partial f} \left[ \frac{ \partial f}{\partial b} \right] = \frac{ \partial f}{\partial c} \frac{1}{2\sqrt{b}} + \frac{ \partial f}{\partial f} 1 & \{ b \mapsto c=\sqrt{b}, b \mapsto f=b+c\} \\ \frac{ \partial f}{\partial a} &= \frac{ \partial f}{\partial b} \left[ \frac{ \partial b}{\partial a} \right] = \frac{ \partial f}{\partial b} y & \{ a \mapsto b=y a\} \\ \frac{ \partial f}{\partial y} &= \frac{ \partial f}{\partial b} \left[ \frac{ \partial b}{\partial y} \right] = \frac{ \partial f}{\partial b} a & \{ y \mapsto b=ya\} \\ \frac{ \partial f}{\partial x} &= \frac{ \partial f}{\partial a} \left[ \frac{ \partial a}{\partial x} \right] = \frac{ \partial f}{\partial a} \frac{1}{x} & \{ x \mapsto a=\log(x)\} \end{aligned}∂f∂f​∂c∂f​∂b∂f​∂a∂f​∂y∂f​∂x∂f​​=1=∂f∂f​[∂c∂f​]=∂f∂f​1=∂c∂f​[∂b∂c​]+∂f∂f​[∂b∂f​]=∂c∂f​2b​1​+∂f∂f​1=∂b∂f​[∂a∂b​]=∂b∂f​y=∂b∂f​[∂y∂b​]=∂b∂f​a=∂a∂f​[∂x∂a​]=∂a∂f​x1​​{c↦f=b+c}{b↦c=b​,b↦f=b+c}{a↦b=ya}{y↦b=ya}{x↦a=log(x)}​

A single reverse traversal computes both derivatives with respect to xxx and yyy, whereas coordinatewise forward mode requires two passes.

15.3.5 Feed-forward Compositions¶

For a feedforward chain, the computed function is the composition

f=ft∘ft−1∘…∘f2∘f1(15.20)f = f_{t} \circ f_{t-1} \circ \ldots \circ f_2 \circ f_1 \tag{15.20}f=ft​∘ft−1​∘…∘f2​∘f1​(15.20)

for functions fk:Rnk−1→Rnkf_k : \mathbb{R}^{n_{k-1}} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{n_{k}}fk​:Rnk−1​→Rnk​.

The forward evaluation starts from x0=x∈Rn0x_0=x \in \mathbb{R}^{n_0}x0​=x∈Rn0​ and computes

∀ k=1,…,t,xk=fk(xk−1)\forall \,k=1, \ldots, t, \quad x_{k} = f_k(x_{k-1})∀k=1,…,t,xk​=fk​(xk−1​)

giving the output f(x)=xtf(x) = x_tf(x)=xt​.

Let Ak:=∂fk(xk−1)∈Rnk×nk−1A_k \mathrel{:=}\partial f_k(x_{k-1}) \in \mathbb{R}^{n_{k} \times n_{k-1}}Ak​:=∂fk​(xk−1​)∈Rnk​×nk−1​ be the Jacobian of the local map. The chain rule gives

∂f(x)=At×At−1×…A2×A1.\partial f(x) = A_{t} \times A_{t-1} \times \ldots A_2 \times A_1.∂f(x)=At​×At−1​×…A2​×A1​.

Forward mode multiplies the Jacobians from right to left, while reverse mode multiplies them from left to right

∂f(x)=At×(At−1×(…×(A3×(A2×A1)))),∂f(x)=((((At×At−1)×At−2)×…)×A2)×A1.\begin{aligned} \partial f(x) &= A_{t} \times \left( A_{t-1} \times \left( \ldots \times \left( A_3 \times \left( A_2 \times A_1 \right) \right) \right) \right), \\ \partial f(x) &= \left( \left( \left( \left( A_{t} \times A_{t-1} \right) \times A_{t-2} \right) \times \ldots \right) \times A_2 \right) \times A_1. \end{aligned}∂f(x)∂f(x)​=At​×(At−1​×(…×(A3​×(A2​×A1​)))),=((((At​×At−1​)×At−2​)×…)×A2​)×A1​.​

Figure 15.11. Matrix multiplication costs for forward mode (left) and reverse mode (right) along a chain.

We note that the computation of the product A×BA \times BA×B of A∈Rn×pA \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}A∈Rn×p with B∈Rp×qB \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times q}B∈Rp×q requires O(npq)O(npq)O(npq) arithmetic operations with the standard dense algorithm.

As shown on Figure 15.11, the arithmetic costs of the two parenthesizations are proportional to

n0∑k=1t−1nknk+1andnt∑k=0t−2nknk+1n_0 \sum_{k=1}^{t-1} n_k n_{k+1} \quad \text{and} \quad n_t \sum_{k=0}^{t-2} n_k n_{k+1}n0​k=1∑t−1​nk​nk+1​andnt​k=0∑t−2​nk​nk+1​

For roughly comparable intermediate widths, these costs favor reverse mode when nt≪n0n_t\ll n_0nt​≪n0​. A scalar learning objective typically has nt=1n_t=1nt​=1, making reverse mode a natural choice; the exact cost comparison depends on all the intermediate dimensions.

15.3.6 Feed-forward Architecture¶

A parameterized feedforward architecture, such as a neural network, has the form

∀ k=1,…,t,xk=fk(xk−1,θk−1)(15.21)\forall \,k=1, \ldots, t, \quad x_{k} = f_k(x_{k-1},\theta_{k-1}) \tag{15.21}∀k=1,…,t,xk​=fk​(xk−1​,θk−1​)(15.21)

where θk−1\theta_{k-1}θk−1​ is the parameter vector for a layer and the input x0∈Rn0x_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{n_0}x0​∈Rn0​ is fixed. The objective is

f(θ):=L(xt)(15.22)f(\theta) \mathrel{:=}L(x_t) \tag{15.22}f(θ):=L(xt​)(15.22)

Here L:Rnt→RL : \mathbb{R}^{n_t} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}L:Rnt​→R is a loss, such as squared prediction error or logistic loss, and θ=(θk)k=0t−1\theta=(\theta_k)_{k=0}^{t-1}θ=(θk​)k=0t−1​ collects the parameters. Figure 15.12 shows the computational graph.

Figure 15.12. Computational graph for a feedforward architecture.

Reverse mode computes the gradient of fff by propagating derivatives through the variables (xk,θk)(x_k,\theta_k)(xk​,θk​). Initialize

∇xtf=∇L(xt)\nabla_{x_t} f = \nabla L(x_t)∇xt​​f=∇L(xt​)

and recurse from k=tk=tk=t down to 1:

zk−1=[∂xfk(xk−1,θk−1)]⊤zkand∇θk−1f=[∂θfk(xk−1,θk−1)]⊤(∇xkf)(15.23)z_{k-1} = [\partial_x f_k(x_{k-1},\theta_{k-1})]^\top z_k \quad \text{and} \quad \nabla_{\theta_{k-1}} f = [\partial_\theta f_k(x_{k-1},\theta_{k-1})]^\top (\nabla_{x_{k}} f) \tag{15.23}zk−1​=[∂x​fk​(xk−1​,θk−1​)]⊤zk​and∇θk−1​​f=[∂θ​fk​(xk−1​,θk−1​)]⊤(∇xk​​f)(15.23)

where zk:=∇xkf(θ)z_k \mathrel{:=}\nabla_{x_{k}} f(\theta)zk​:=∇xk​​f(θ) is the gradient with respect to xkx_{k}xk​.

Multilayer perceptrons.

For a fully connected network without biases, use

∀ xk−1∈Rnk−1,fk(xk−1,θk−1)=ρ(θk−1xk−1)(15.24)\forall \,x_{k-1} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_{k-1}}, \quad f_k(x_{k-1},\theta_{k-1}) = \rho( \theta_{k-1} x_{k-1} ) \tag{15.24}∀xk−1​∈Rnk−1​,fk​(xk−1​,θk−1​)=ρ(θk−1​xk−1​)(15.24)

where θk−1∈Rnk×nk−1\theta_{k-1}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_k\times n_{k-1}}θk−1​∈Rnk​×nk−1​ contains the weights and ρ\rhoρ acts coordinatewise; see Figure 15.13. The derivative formulas below apply where ρ\rhoρ is differentiable. At a ReLU kink, a chosen derivative convention defines the computed update, but the classical derivative need not exist.

For an adjoint vector zk∈Rnkz_k \in \mathbb{R}^{n_k}zk​∈Rnk​, typically ∇xkf\nabla_{x_{k}} f∇xk​​f,

{[∂xfk(xk−1,θk−1)]⊤(zk)=θk−1⊤wkzk,[∂θfk(xk−1,θk−1)]⊤(zk)=(wkzk)xk−1⊤wherewk:=diag(ρ′(θk−1xk−1)).\left\{ \begin{matrix} [\partial_x f_k(x_{k-1},\theta_{k-1})]^\top (z_k) = \theta_{k-1}^\top w_k z_k, \\ [\partial_\theta f_k(x_{k-1},\theta_{k-1})]^\top (z_k) =(w_kz_k)x_{k-1}^\top \end{matrix} \right. \quad \text{where} \quad w_k \mathrel{:=}\mathop{\mathrm{diag}}(\rho'(\theta_{k-1} x_{k-1})).{[∂x​fk​(xk−1​,θk−1​)]⊤(zk​)=θk−1⊤​wk​zk​,[∂θ​fk​(xk−1​,θk−1​)]⊤(zk​)=(wk​zk​)xk−1⊤​​wherewk​:=diag(ρ′(θk−1​xk−1​)).

Link with adjoint state method.

A residual form of (15.21) can be interpreted as a time discretization of an ordinary differential equation.

Keep the state dimension fixed, nk=nn_k=nnk​=n, and interpret xkx_kxk​ as an approximation of a continuous trajectory x(t)x(t)x(t) at time t=kτt=k\taut=kτ. The formal continuum limit takes τ↓0\tau\downarrow0τ↓0 with kτk\taukτ approaching a fixed time.

Impose the residual structure

fk(xk−1,θk−1)=xk−1+τu(xk−1,θk−1,kτ)(15.25)f_k(x_{k-1},\theta_{k-1}) = x_{k-1} + \tau u(x_{k-1},\theta_{k-1}, k\tau) \tag{15.25}fk​(xk−1​,θk−1​)=xk−1​+τu(xk−1​,θk−1​,kτ)(15.25)

with a parameterized vector field u(x,θ,t)∈Rnu(x,\theta,t) \in \mathbb{R}^nu(x,θ,t)∈Rn. Formally, as τ→0\tau \rightarrow 0τ→0, this approaches the nonlinear ODE

x˙(t)=u(x(t),θ(t),t)(15.26)\dot x(t) = u(x(t),\theta(t),t) \tag{15.26}x˙(t)=u(x(t),θ(t),t)(15.26)

with x(t=0)=x0x(t=0)=x_0x(t=0)=x0​.

Writing z(t)=∇x(t)f(θ)z(t) = \nabla_{x(t)} f(\theta)z(t)=∇x(t)​f(θ) for the adjoint, the discrete relations (15.23) become a linear backward ODE:

z˙(t)=−[∂xu(x(t),θ(t),t)]⊤z(t)and∇θ(t)f(θ)=[∂θu(x(t),θ(t),t)]⊤z(t).\dot z(t) = - [\partial_x u(x(t),\theta(t),t)]^\top z(t) \quad \text{and} \quad \nabla_{\theta(t)} f(\theta) = [\partial_\theta u(x(t),\theta(t),t)]^\top z(t).z˙(t)=−[∂x​u(x(t),θ(t),t)]⊤z(t)and∇θ(t)​f(θ)=[∂θ​u(x(t),θ(t),t)]⊤z(t).

The adjoint has terminal condition z(T)=∇L(x(T))z(T)=\nabla L(x(T))z(T)=∇L(x(T)). The parameter derivative is interpreted as the L2L^2L2 functional gradient with respect to the time-dependent control. **Residual recurrent networks. **

A residual recurrent network uses the update

h(x,θ)=x+W2⊤ρ(W1x)h(x,\theta) = x + W_2^\top \rho( W_1 x )h(x,θ)=x+W2⊤​ρ(W1​x)

as illustrated in Figure 15.15. Here θ=(W1,W2)∈(Rq×n)2\theta= (W_1, W_2) \in (\mathbb{R}^{q\times n})^2θ=(W1​,W2​)∈(Rq×n)2 contains the weights and ρ\rhoρ is a pointwise activation. Increasing the hidden width qqq enlarges the class of representable residual maps.

When W2=−τW1W_2=-\tau W_1W2​=−τW1​ and ρ=ψ′\rho=\psi'ρ=ψ′, this update is a gradient step for E(x,θ)=∑iψ((W1x)i)\mathcal{E}(x,\theta)=\sum_i\psi((W_1x)_i)E(x,θ)=∑i​ψ((W1​x)i​). Repeating it gives an iterative implementation of the argmin layer (15.31), provided the iterations converge to a minimizer.

The Jacobians ∂θh\partial_\theta h∂θ​h and ∂xh\partial_x h∂x​h follow from the layer formulas in the multilayer-perceptron discussion.

**Mitigating Memory Requirements. **

Backpropagation requires access to the iterates (xk)k=0t(x_k)_{k=0}^t(xk​)k=0t​, whose storage can dominate memory use. Checkpointing stores selected states and reruns parts of the forward computation to reconstruct missing values. Recursive schedules can use O(log⁡t)O(\log t)O(logt) stored states with an O(log⁡t)O(\log t)O(logt) computational overhead.

If the forward computation is invertible, stored states can sometimes be reconstructed instead. Assume maps gkg_kgk​ satisfy

xk=gk(xk+1,…,xt).x_{k} = g_k(x_{k+1},\ldots,x_t).xk​=gk​(xk+1​,…,xt​).

These inverse updates may amplify numerical errors, so algebraic invertibility alone does not ensure stable reconstruction. In practice, the inverse can also depend on a few extra variables, in particular on the input values (x0,…,xs)(x_0,\ldots,x_s)(x0​,…,xs​).

For example, split the continuous state as x(t)=(r(t),s(t))x(t)=(r(t),s(t))x(t)=(r(t),s(t)) and suppose the vector field in (15.26) has the separated form u((r,s),θ,t)=(F(s,θ,t),G(r,θ,t))u((r,s),\theta,t)=(F(s,\theta,t),G(r,\theta,t))u((r,s),θ,t)=(F(s,θ,t),G(r,θ,t)). An invertible staggered update is

rk+1=rk+τF(sk,θk,τk)andsk+1=sk+τG(rk+1,θk+1/2,τ(k+1/2)).r_{k+1} = r_k + \tau F(s_k,\theta_k,\tau k) \quad \text{and} \quad s_{k+1} = s_k + \tau G(r_{k+1},\theta_{k+1/2},\tau (k+1/2)).rk+1​=rk​+τF(sk​,θk​,τk)andsk+1​=sk​+τG(rk+1​,θk+1/2​,τ(k+1/2)).

In exact arithmetic, these updates can be inverted as

sk=sk+1−τG(rk+1,θk+1/2,τ(k+1/2)).andrk=rk+1−τF(sk,θk,τk).s_k = s_{k+1} - \tau G(r_{k+1},\theta_{k+1/2},\tau (k+1/2)). \quad \text{and} \quad r_k = r_{k+1} - \tau F(s_k,\theta_k,\tau k).sk​=sk+1​−τG(rk+1​,θk+1/2​,τ(k+1/2)).andrk​=rk+1​−τF(sk​,θk​,τk).

Fixed point maps

If hhh is continuous and the iterates converge to x⋆(θ)x^\star(\theta)x⋆(θ), their limit is a fixed point:

x⋆(θ)=h(x⋆(θ),θ).x^\star(\theta) = h(x^\star(\theta),\theta).x⋆(θ)=h(x⋆(θ),θ).

Backpropagation differentiates the finite computation f(θ)=L(xt,θ)f(\theta) = L(x_t,\theta)f(θ)=L(xt​,θ). For the limiting objective f⋆(θ)=L(x⋆(θ),θ)f^\star(\theta) = L(x^\star(\theta),\theta)f⋆(θ)=L(x⋆(θ),θ), the implicit function theorem gives an alternative:

∇f⋆(θ)=[∂x⋆(θ)]⊤(∇xL(x⋆(θ),θ))+∇θL(x⋆(θ),θ).(15.30)\nabla f^\star(\theta) = [\partial x^\star(\theta)]^\top( \nabla_x L(x^\star(\theta),\theta) ) + \nabla_\theta L(x^\star(\theta),\theta). \tag{15.30}∇f⋆(θ)=[∂x⋆(θ)]⊤(∇x​L(x⋆(θ),θ))+∇θ​L(x⋆(θ),θ).(15.30)

Assume hhh is continuously differentiable and Id−∂xh\mathrm{Id}-\partial_xhId−∂x​h is invertible at the fixed point. The implicit function theorem then gives

∂x⋆(θ)=(Id−∂xh(x⋆(θ),θ))−1∂θh(x⋆(θ),θ).\partial x^\star(\theta)=\left(\mathrm{Id}-\partial_xh(x^\star(\theta),\theta)\right)^{-1}\partial_\theta h(x^\star(\theta),\theta).∂x⋆(θ)=(Id−∂x​h(x⋆(θ),θ))−1∂θ​h(x⋆(θ),θ).

In practice, one replaces in these formulas x⋆(θ)x^\star(\theta)x⋆(θ) by xtx_txt​, which approximates the derivative of the converged objective f⋆f^\starf⋆, rather than the derivative of the finite unrolling fff.

This approach replaces storage of the iteration history by a linear solve at the approximate equilibrium.

Argmin layers

An argmin layer maps a parameter θ\thetaθ to a minimizer x(θ)x(\theta)x(θ) of a parameterized objective. Assume a unique minimizer, or specify a branch when several exist:

x(θ)=argminx  E(x,θ).x(\theta) = \underset{x}{\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}}\; \mathcal{E}(x,\theta).x(θ)=xargmin​E(x,θ).

One way to compute the layer is gradient descent, initialized here at x0=0x_0=0x0​=0:

xk+1=xk−τ∇E(xk,θ).(15.31)x_{k+1} = x_k - \tau \nabla \mathcal{E}(x_k,\theta). \tag{15.31}xk+1​=xk​−τ∇E(xk​,θ).(15.31)

This has the form (15.25) when using the vector field u(x,θ)=−∇xE(x,θ)u(x,\theta)=-\nabla_x\mathcal{E}(x,\theta)u(x,θ)=−∇x​E(x,θ).

Assume E\mathcal{E}E is twice continuously differentiable near the selected minimizer and its Hessian with respect to xxx is invertible. The implicit function theorem gives a locally differentiable minimizer branch; applying (15.30) to its stationarity equation yields

∇f⋆(θ)=−(∂2E∂x∂θ(x⋆(θ),θ))⊤(∂2E∂x2(x⋆(θ),θ))−1(∇xL(x⋆(θ),θ))+∇θL(x⋆(θ),θ)\nabla f^\star(\theta) = -\left( \frac{\partial^2 \mathcal{E}}{\partial x \partial \theta}(x^\star(\theta),\theta) \right)^\top \left( \frac{ \partial^2 \mathcal{E}}{\partial x^2} (x^\star(\theta),\theta) \right)^{-1} ( \nabla_x L(x^\star(\theta),\theta) ) + \nabla_\theta L(x^\star(\theta),\theta)∇f⋆(θ)=−(∂x∂θ∂2E​(x⋆(θ),θ))⊤(∂x2∂2E​(x⋆(θ),θ))−1(∇x​L(x⋆(θ),θ))+∇θ​L(x⋆(θ),θ)

If f(θ)f(\theta)f(θ) is the minimized value itself, f(θ)=E(x⋆(θ),θ)f(\theta)=\mathcal{E}(x^\star(\theta),\theta)f(θ)=E(x⋆(θ),θ), then L=EL=\mathcal{E}L=E. Formula (15.30) simplifies because ∇xL(x⋆(θ),θ)=0\nabla_x L(x^\star(\theta),\theta)=0∇x​L(x⋆(θ),θ)=0, giving

∇f⋆(θ)=∇θL(x⋆(θ),θ).(15.32)\nabla f^\star(\theta) = \nabla_\theta L(x^\star(\theta),\theta). \tag{15.32}∇f⋆(θ)=∇θ​L(x⋆(θ),θ).(15.32)

This is the envelope theorem, also associated with Danskin’s theorem.

Sinkhorn’s algorithm

Let a∈Rna\in\mathbb{R}^na∈Rn and b∈Rmb\in\mathbb{R}^mb∈Rm be strictly positive probability vectors, let C∈Rn×mC\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}C∈Rn×m be a cost matrix, and let ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0. Entropic optimal transport minimizes

∑ijCijPij+ε∑ijPij(log⁡Pij−1)\sum_{ij}C_{ij}P_{ij}+\varepsilon\sum_{ij}P_{ij}(\log P_{ij}-1)ij∑​Cij​Pij​+εij∑​Pij​(logPij​−1)

over P⩾0P\geqslant 0P⩾0 with row sums aaa and column sums bbb. Set Kij=e−Cij/ε>0K_{ij}=e^{-C_{ij}/\varepsilon}>0Kij​=e−Cij​/ε>0. Sinkhorn’s alternating updates, initialized with positive scaling vectors, are

uk+1=aKvk,vk+1=bK⊤uk+1.u_{k+1}=\frac{a}{Kv_k},\qquad v_{k+1}=\frac{b}{K^\top u_{k+1}}.uk+1​=Kvk​a​,vk+1​=K⊤uk+1​b​.

All divisions are componentwise. The second update uses the newly computed uk+1u_{k+1}uk+1​; this sequential dependence is part of Sinkhorn’s alternating scheme.

The regularized transport value is the maximum of the dual objective

E(u,v;a,b)=ε(⟨a, log⁡u⟩+⟨b, log⁡v⟩−⟨u, Kv⟩).\mathcal{E}(u,v;a,b)=\varepsilon\left(\langle a,\,\log u\rangle+\langle b,\,\log v\rangle-\langle u,\,Kv\rangle\right).E(u,v;a,b)=ε(⟨a,logu⟩+⟨b,logv⟩−⟨u,Kv⟩).

Sinkhorn performs alternating maximization of this objective. A finite number of iterations defines a differentiable recurrent map on positive inputs. Its Jacobian products can be computed by chaining the two scaling steps. For example, for u=a/(Kv)u=a/(Kv)u=a/(Kv),

∂vu=−diag(a(Kv)2)K,∂au=diag(1Kv),\partial_vu=-\mathop{\mathrm{diag}}\left(\frac{a}{(Kv)^2}\right)K,\qquad \partial_au=\mathop{\mathrm{diag}}\left(\frac1{Kv}\right),∂v​u=−diag((Kv)2a​)K,∂a​u=diag(Kv1​),

and analogous formulas apply to the vvv update, with the dependence through the newly computed uuu included.

At convergence, the envelope theorem gives marginal derivatives represented by the dual potentials

∇af⋆=εlog⁡u⋆,∇bf⋆=εlog⁡v⋆.\nabla_a f^\star=\varepsilon\log u^\star,\qquad \nabla_b f^\star=\varepsilon\log v^\star.∇a​f⋆=εlogu⋆,∇b​f⋆=εlogv⋆.

The scalings have the invariance (u,v)↦(cu,v/c)(u,v)\mapsto(cu,v/c)(u,v)↦(cu,v/c), so these potentials are defined up to opposite additive constants. On the probability simplices, derivatives act on zero-sum perturbations and are therefore independent of this gauge. An implicit differentiation formula must fix the gauge before inverting a Jacobian; the unmodified fixed-point Jacobian is singular in that direction.
